notes.definition: Diffusion is the spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
explanation: Particles in liquids and gases are constantly moving randomly. Where there are lots of particles (a high concentration), more of them move away than move in, so overall they spread out into areas where there are fewer particles. This overall movement is called net movement, and it is always from higher to lower concentration, down a concentration gradient. Diffusion is passive: it does not need energy from respiration, because it relies on the particles' own random movement. Substances can diffuse into and out of cells across the cell membrane, as long as their particles are small enough to pass through.

Many important substances move into and out of cells by diffusion. In gas exchange, oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. In respiring cells oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide diffuses out. In leaves, carbon dioxide diffuses in through the stomata for photosynthesis and oxygen diffuses out. The waste product urea diffuses from cells into the blood plasma, which carries it to the kidneys for excretion.

Three factors affect the rate of diffusion. First, the difference in concentrations (the concentration gradient): the steeper the gradient, the faster the rate. Second, the temperature: at higher temperatures particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so diffusion is faster. Third, the surface area of the membrane: a larger surface area means more particles can cross at the same time. Distance also matters: a thinner membrane gives a shorter diffusion path, so diffusion across it is faster.

A single-celled organism, such as an amoeba, has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio (SA:V). This allows enough oxygen, food molecules and waste to move into and out of the cell by diffusion across its surface to meet its needs. As an object gets bigger, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so its SA:V ratio decreases. To calculate SA:V for a cube, find the total surface area (6 × side²) and the volume (side³), then divide surface area by volume and write the answer as a ratio such as 3 : 1.

Large multicellular organisms have a small SA:V ratio. Their outer surface is too small for diffusion to supply all their cells, and the distances from the surface to the inner cells are too long. So they have specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. The effectiveness of an exchange surface is increased by: having a large surface area; having a membrane that is thin, to give a short diffusion path; in animals, having an efficient blood supply, which keeps the concentration gradient steep; and, in animals for gaseous exchange, being ventilated.

In the lungs, millions of alveoli give a huge surface area. Their walls and the capillary walls are each one cell thick, a dense capillary network carries oxygen away quickly, and breathing ventilates the alveoli. In the small intestine, villi (and microvilli on their cells) increase the surface area, the villus wall is one cell thick and each villus has a good blood supply to carry absorbed products away. Fish gills have many thin filaments covered in lamellae, giving a large surface area, with a thin surface, many capillaries, and a constant flow of water over them.

Plants have exchange surfaces too. Leaves are broad and flat, giving a large surface area, and thin, so gases have only a short distance to diffuse. Stomata let carbon dioxide diffuse in and oxygen and water vapour diffuse out, and air spaces in the spongy mesophyll give a large internal surface area. In roots, root hair cells greatly increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.
keyFacts: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher concentration to a lower concentration.
Diffusion is passive: it does not need energy from respiration.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide move by diffusion in gas exchange; urea diffuses from cells into the blood plasma.
Rate of diffusion increases with a steeper concentration gradient, a higher temperature and a larger surface area.
A thinner membrane gives a shorter diffusion path and faster diffusion.
Single-celled organisms have a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion across their surface meets their needs.
As size increases, the surface area to volume ratio decreases.
Exchange surfaces are made more effective by a large surface area, a thin membrane, an efficient blood supply and ventilation.
Alveoli, villi, gill filaments, root hair cells and leaves are all adapted for exchanging materials.

keyTerms.definition: The spreading out of particles of a substance in solution or a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
The difference in concentration between two areas. Diffusion happens down a concentration gradient.
The overall movement of particles in one direction, after taking into account random movement in both directions.
The surface area of an object divided by its volume (SA:V). Smaller objects have larger ratios.
A specialised surface where substances are exchanged between an organism and its environment, such as alveoli, villi or gills.
The distance particles must travel by diffusion. A shorter path gives faster diffusion.
Moving air or water over a gas exchange surface, which keeps the concentration gradient steep.
A waste product that diffuses from cells into the blood plasma and is removed by the kidneys.

equations.name: Surface area to volume ratio
equations.formula: SA:V = surface area ÷ volume, written as a ratio n : 1

workedExamples.title: SA:V of a cube
workedExamples.question: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 2 cm.
steps: Area of one face = 2 × 2 = 4 cm². A cube has 6 faces, so surface area = 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

workedExamples.title: SA:V of a cuboid
workedExamples.question: A block of agar measures 1 cm × 2 cm × 4 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio.
steps: The cuboid has three pairs of faces: 1 × 2 = 2 cm², 1 × 4 = 4 cm² and 2 × 4 = 8 cm².

workedExamples.title: Comparing two organisms
workedExamples.question: A cube-shaped single cell has sides of 10 μm. A cube-shaped multicellular organism has sides of 1000 μm. Compare their SA:V ratios.
steps: 0.6 ÷ 0.006 = 100, so the single cell has a ratio 100 times larger.
workedExamples.answer: Cell 0.6 : 1; organism 0.006 : 1. The single cell's SA:V is 100 times larger, so diffusion across its surface can meet its needs, but the larger organism needs exchange surfaces and transport systems.

workedExamples.title: Rate of diffusion
workedExamples.question: Dye diffuses 12 mm into a block of agar in 30 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of diffusion in mm per minute.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think particles stop moving once they are evenly spread out.
misconceptions.right: In fact particles keep moving randomly; there is just no longer any net movement in one direction.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think diffusion needs energy from the cell.
misconceptions.right: In fact diffusion is passive. It depends on the random movement of particles, so no energy from respiration is needed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say particles move 'along' or 'across' a concentration gradient without giving the direction.
misconceptions.right: In fact you should say particles move from a higher to a lower concentration, which is 'down' the concentration gradient.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think bigger organisms have a bigger surface area to volume ratio because they have more surface.
misconceptions.right: In fact bigger organisms have more surface area in total, but their volume increases even faster, so their SA:V ratio is smaller.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think only gases diffuse.
misconceptions.right: In fact particles of any substance in solution can diffuse too, for example glucose and urea dissolved in water.

realWorld: People with emphysema have damaged alveolar walls, which reduces the surface area of the lungs, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood and they become breathless.
Coeliac disease damages the villi in the small intestine, reducing the surface area for absorption and causing poor absorption of food molecules.
Fish can suffocate in warm, still water because it holds less dissolved oxygen, reducing the concentration gradient across the gills.
Kidney dialysis machines use diffusion: urea diffuses out of the blood across a thin membrane into dialysis fluid that contains no urea.
examTips: Always say 'from a higher concentration to a lower concentration' and include the word 'net' in definitions to get full marks.
In SA:V calculations, show surface area and volume separately with units, then give the ratio in the form n : 1.

When explaining an exchange surface, link each feature to its effect: large surface area (more particles cross at once), thin (short diffusion path), blood supply or ventilation (maintains a steep concentration gradient).
If asked why temperature increases diffusion, mention that particles have more kinetic energy and move faster.
Remember that a large organism has a SMALLER SA:V ratio, which is why it needs exchange surfaces and a transport system.
summary: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration; it is passive.
Oxygen, carbon dioxide and urea are examples of substances that diffuse into or out of cells.
Rate of diffusion depends on concentration gradient, temperature and surface area.
Small organisms have a large SA:V ratio, so diffusion across their surface is enough.
Large organisms need exchange surfaces: large area, thin, good blood supply and ventilation.
Lungs, small intestine, gills, roots and leaves are all adapted for efficient exchange.

Name three substances that move by diffusion in the body.
Name three factors that affect the rate of diffusion.
flashcards.back: Concentration gradient, temperature and surface area of the membrane.

flashcards.front: Why does a higher temperature increase the rate of diffusion?
flashcards.back: Particles have more kinetic energy so move faster.

flashcards.front: Why do single-celled organisms not need exchange surfaces?
flashcards.back: They have a large SA:V ratio, so diffusion across the cell surface meets their needs.

flashcards.front: What happens to SA:V as an organism gets bigger?
flashcards.back: It decreases, because volume increases faster than surface area.

flashcards.front: Four features of an effective exchange surface
flashcards.back: Large surface area; thin membrane (short diffusion path); efficient blood supply; ventilation (for gas exchange in animals).

flashcards.front: How are alveoli adapted for gas exchange?
flashcards.back: Huge surface area, walls one cell thick, rich capillary network, ventilated by breathing.

flashcards.front: How are villi adapted for absorption?
flashcards.back: Large surface area (with microvilli), wall one cell thick, good blood supply.

flashcards.front: How are fish gills adapted for gas exchange?
flashcards.back: Many filaments with lamellae (large surface area), thin surface, many capillaries, water constantly flows over them.

flashcards.front: How are leaves adapted for gas exchange?
flashcards.back: Broad and flat (large surface area), thin (short path), stomata, and air spaces in the spongy mesophyll.

flashcards.front: Where does urea diffuse to and from?
flashcards.back: From cells into the blood plasma, for excretion by the kidneys.

questions.question: Which statement describes diffusion?
options: Net movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration
Net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
Movement of water only, through a partially permeable membrane
Movement of particles using energy from respiration
markScheme: 1 mark: net movement from higher to lower concentration
questions.explanation: Diffusion is net movement from a higher to a lower concentration. Movement from lower to higher concentration using energy is active transport; water moving through a partially permeable membrane is osmosis.

markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Arrow X points from the blood into the alveolus. Blood arriving at the lungs has a high carbon dioxide concentration, so carbon dioxide diffuses into the alveoli to be breathed out. Oxygen diffuses the other way.

questions.question: Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
markScheme: 1 mark: increasing the temperature
questions.explanation: At higher temperatures particles have more kinetic energy and move faster. The other changes would all slow diffusion down.

questions.question: Which waste product diffuses from cells into the blood plasma to be removed by the kidneys?
markScheme: 1 mark: urea
questions.explanation: Urea is a waste product that diffuses from cells into the blood plasma and is excreted by the kidneys. Glucose, oxygen and amino acids are useful substances, not waste.

questions.question: Which feature of the alveoli helps to keep a steep concentration gradient of oxygen?
options: A good blood supply that carries oxygen away
markScheme: 1 mark: a good blood supply that carries oxygen away
questions.explanation: Blood flowing through the capillaries carries oxygenated blood away and brings deoxygenated blood, keeping the oxygen concentration in the blood low and the gradient steep. Thin walls shorten the diffusion path but do not maintain the gradient.

questions.question: Why does an amoeba not need a specialised gas exchange surface?
options: It has a small surface area to volume ratio
It has a large surface area to volume ratio
It gets oxygen by active transport
markScheme: 1 mark: it has a large surface area to volume ratio
questions.explanation: A single-celled organism has a relatively large SA:V ratio, so diffusion across its surface supplies enough oxygen. It still respires, and oxygen enters by diffusion, not active transport.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows two cubes, A and B.
The sides of cube B are twice as long as the sides of cube A.
What happens to the surface area to volume ratio when the length of the sides is doubled?

markScheme: 1 mark: it halves
questions.explanation: Surface area increases by 2² = 4 times and volume by 2³ = 8 times, so SA:V changes by 4 ÷ 8 = ½. For example, 1 cm cube is 6 : 1 and 2 cm cube is 3 : 1.

questions.question: Fish gills stick together and collapse when a fish is taken out of water. Why does this stop gas exchange working effectively?
options: The surface area for diffusion is greatly reduced
The gills start to use active transport instead
The blood supply to the gills increases
markScheme: 1 mark: the surface area for diffusion is greatly reduced
questions.explanation: In water the filaments and lamellae are held apart, giving a large surface area. Out of water they collapse together, so much less surface is available for oxygen to diffuse across.

questions.question: Through which structures does carbon dioxide diffuse into a leaf?
markScheme: 1 mark: stomata
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf through the stomata, the pores mainly on the underside of the leaf. Xylem carries water, and root hairs are in the roots.

questions.question:
A cube of agar has sides of 1 cm.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the cube.
Give your answer in the form x : 1
markScheme: 1 mark: SA = 6 × 1 × 1 = 6 cm² and V = 1 cm³
1 mark: ratio = 6 : 1
questions.explanation: Each face is 1 cm², and there are 6 faces, so SA = 6 cm². Volume = 1 cm³. 6 ÷ 1 = 6, so the ratio is 6 : 1.

questions.question:
A student placed a cube of pink agar into acid. As the acid diffused into the agar, it turned the agar colourless.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the mean rate of diffusion of the acid in mm per minute.

headers: Distance acid diffused into agar in mm

markScheme: 1 mark: 9 ÷ 15 = 0.6 mm/min
questions.explanation: Rate = distance ÷ time = 9 ÷ 15 = 0.6 mm per minute.

questions.question:
A cube-shaped cell has sides of 20 μm.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the cell.
Give your answer in the form x : 1
markScheme: 1 mark: SA = 6 × 20² = 2400 μm²
1 mark: V = 20³ = 8000 μm³
questions.explanation: SA = 6 × 400 = 2400 μm². V = 20 × 20 × 20 = 8000 μm³. 2400 ÷ 8000 = 0.3. For any cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side, and 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3, which confirms the answer.

questions.question: Name the gas that diffuses from the alveoli into the blood.
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: Air in the alveoli has a higher oxygen concentration than the blood, so oxygen diffuses into the blood.

questions.question: Give two factors that affect the rate of diffusion.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: concentration gradient (difference in concentrations) / temperature / surface area of the membrane
questions.explanation: The AQA specification lists the concentration gradient, temperature and surface area of the membrane. A thinner membrane (shorter path) also speeds diffusion.

questions.question: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of diffusion.
markScheme: 1 mark: particles have more kinetic energy
1 mark: so they move faster / more particles cross the membrane per second
questions.explanation: Heating gives particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and spread out more quickly.

questions.question: Explain how the villi in the small intestine are adapted for efficient absorption.
markScheme: 1 mark: villi (and microvilli) give a large surface area
1 mark: wall is one cell thick / thin, giving a short diffusion path
1 mark: good blood supply carries absorbed molecules away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Each feature speeds up diffusion: a larger area lets more molecules cross at once, a thin wall shortens the path, and the blood supply keeps the gradient steep.

questions.question: Explain why a large multicellular organism, such as a mammal, needs specialised exchange surfaces.
acceptedAnswers: small surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: it has a small surface area to volume ratio
1 mark: so diffusion across its outer surface would be too slow / the distance to inner cells is too great to meet its needs
questions.explanation: As organisms get bigger their SA:V ratio falls, so their outer surface cannot supply enough oxygen and nutrients by diffusion alone.

questions.question: Describe how leaves are adapted for gas exchange.
markScheme: 1 mark: broad and flat, giving a large surface area / air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
1 mark: thin, giving a short diffusion path / stomata allow gases in and out
questions.explanation: Leaves have a large surface area and are thin; stomata let carbon dioxide diffuse in and oxygen diffuse out, and internal air spaces give a large surface for exchange.

questions.question: Explain why ventilation of the lungs increases the rate of oxygen diffusion into the blood.
markScheme: 1 mark: breathing brings in fresh air with a high oxygen concentration
1 mark: and removes air with less oxygen / more carbon dioxide
1 mark: so a steep concentration gradient is maintained between the alveoli and the blood
questions.explanation: Without ventilation, the air in the alveoli would lose oxygen and the gradient would get smaller, slowing diffusion. Breathing keeps replacing it.

questions.question:
Diffusion is a passive process.
Explain what is meant by passive and why diffusion is passive.
markScheme: 1 mark: it does not require energy from respiration
1 mark: because it relies on the random movement (kinetic energy) of the particles themselves
questions.explanation: Passive means the cell does not have to supply energy. The particles move on their own because of their kinetic energy.

questions.question: Describe the direction in which particles move overall during diffusion.
markScheme: 1 mark: from a higher concentration to a lower concentration / down the concentration gradient
questions.explanation: The net movement in diffusion is from where particles are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

questions.question: Compare how the lungs of a mammal and the gills of a fish are adapted for efficient gas exchange.
markScheme: Indicative content. Similarities: both have a large surface area; lungs have millions of alveoli; gills have many filaments with lamellae; both have a thin exchange surface / short diffusion path; alveolar and capillary walls one cell thick; lamellae thin; both have an efficient blood supply / many capillaries that maintain the concentration gradient; both are ventilated. Differences: lungs ventilated by breathing air in and out; gills ventilated by a constant one-way flow of water; oxygen comes from air in lungs but from water (dissolved oxygen) in gills; gill filaments need water to stay apart.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison covering surface area, thinness, blood supply and ventilation for both organs, linking features to faster diffusion, with at least one difference.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes several features of both organs with some links to diffusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple features of one or both organs, with few links to diffusion.
questions.explanation: Both organs show the four features of an effective exchange surface. Strong answers compare them directly, explain how each feature speeds diffusion, and note differences such as air versus water ventilation.

questions.question:
A student placed three cubes of pink indicator agar into acid. The cubes had sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm.
The acid turns the agar colourless as it diffuses in.
Table 1 shows the time taken for each cube to become completely colourless.
Explain these results.
Use surface area to volume ratios in your answer.

headers: Length of side of cube in cm
Time to become colourless in minutes

markScheme: Indicative content: SA:V of 1 cm cube = 6 : 1; 2 cm cube = 3 : 1; 3 cm cube = 2 : 1; smaller cube has the largest SA:V; more surface for acid to enter relative to the volume to be filled; and the distance to the centre is shorter (0.5 cm compared with 1.5 cm); so the whole volume becomes colourless sooner; this models why small organisms can rely on diffusion but large organisms need exchange surfaces.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct SA:V values for at least two cubes linked clearly to the order of results, including the idea of distance to the centre or the relative volume to fill.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement that smaller cubes have a larger SA:V or change colour faster, with limited calculation or explanation.
questions.explanation: The smallest cube has the largest SA:V (6 : 1 compared with 2 : 1), so it has proportionally more surface for acid to enter and a shorter distance to the centre. This links directly to why single-celled organisms can rely on diffusion.

questions.question:
A cube has a surface area of 96 cm² and a volume of 64 cm³.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the cube.
Give your answer in the form x : 1
questions.explanation: SA:V = 96 ÷ 64 = 1.5. Check: this is a 4 cm cube (6 × 16 = 96, 4³ = 64) and 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.

questions.question: A drop of ink is added to a beaker of still water. After a day the colour is evenly spread. Which statement is correct?
options: All the ink particles have stopped moving
Ink particles are still moving, but there is no net movement
The ink moved by active transport
The water particles moved but the ink particles did not
markScheme: 1 mark: ink particles are still moving, but there is no net movement
questions.explanation: Particles never stop moving randomly. Once the concentration is the same everywhere, equal numbers move in every direction, so there is no net movement.
